claim_verdicts.reason: E2 states that classification, implementation and full migration are separate denominators; E1 fixes the 2,200-service/70-domain figure as a classification result.
E1 gives one accountable model owner and one accepted vocabulary, and E2 gives a single decision authority for each invariant.
E1 requires the module that owns writes to each logical aggregate or table; E2 says separate databases do not prove exclusive authority and E4 covers cache/projection staleness.
E1 defines the five boundaries separately and E2 says they are not the same, so grouping alone does not establish ownership.
E3 states one domain can contain a single service or many; E1 allows multiple organizational teams, E2 warns that reporting structure can split a capability, and E4 names a stable ownership level.

E2 states the owner can replace, split or consolidate services behind a gateway while maintaining caller-visible semantics; E1 defines the stable entry interface hiding internal services, tables and pipelines.
E1 names gateway bypass, over-broad shared DTOs and non-versioned response semantics as recreating direct consumer coupling; E3 adds preservation of the old source-of-truth coupling.

E1 defines gateway aggregation as composing several owner responses, which supports the contrast with internal tables, but no supplied quote states that the result has no single semantic owner; that element is missing.
E1 states a gateway cannot certify object ownership or replace backend authorization; E2 and E3 place object-level authorization at the resource-owning authority.
E1 gives per-dependency deadline and authorization; E2 caps retries and exposes the failing dependency; E3 requires a versioned partial shape; E4 treats gateway outage as its own failure domain.
E3 makes versioning and rollback part of the change; E1 preserves the authoritative store, E2 says a call-graph swap is not a functional contract, and E4 preserves caller-visible semantics.
E2 requires a compatible period, observed consumers and proof of cutover; E1 inventories dependent clients and E3 retires direct dependencies only after measured usage has ceased.
E3 says deploying the new producer is not evidence the old contract disappeared; E1 rejects decreeing universal gateways and E2 rejects a call-graph picture as a functional contract.
E2 states unbounded plugins can change latency, fault isolation and safety behavior despite a stable API; E1 requires a typed provider/plugin interface at a documented extension point.

E1 supports serving explicit integrations without every team editing the same microservices, but E2 attaches the documented exception mechanism to the gateway owner, not to extensions; the extension-specific exception contract is missing.
E1 states serialized payloads still require schema/version, authentication, size, privacy and retention controls.
E1 limits the figure to historical cataloguing scope at the observation date and E2 is the excluded 'already migrated or uniform size' reading listed in the same limits table.
E1 supports partial rollout with other domains still planned and E2 is the excluded 100% organization-wide transition reading in the same limits table.
E1 identifies company-reported improvements for the context, E2 a named experience rather than a randomized comparison, and E3 a source-reported fleet-churn estimate.
E2 requires the observation window, population and confidence caveats with any percentage; E1 lists the absent control cohorts, independent p99 and velocity model in the limits section.
E1 says company-reported and not independently reproduced; E2 forbids extrapolating the dated deployment and E3 records technical review as pending.
The five rows E1-E5 answer the five contract questions: functional ownership, state authority, API/event semantics, security/operations, and failure/recovery.
E1 states hidden coupling produced networked-monolith behavior despite independent deployability; E2 frames the aim as ownership, blast radius and allowed dependencies.
E1 favors domains for a preexisting large fleet with coordination cost; E2 requires a baseline and measurable gates; E3 says not a universal preferred architecture.
E1 says additional gateways can become central points of change; E3 adds error budgets, runbooks, incident ownership and cost; E2 treats the gateway outage as a failure domain.
E2 states a boundary is weak if none of its business rules can be stated separately; E1 says a shared word should not force a shared schema.
E1 restricts offloading to shared, cross-cutting, edge-enforceable functions and names domain-state and blocking-edge contraindications; E2 requires an owner, versioned policy and failure mode.

E1 supports the claim that a stable API does not bound latency, fault isolation or safety, but the specific resource, time, concurrency, isolation, failure and kill-switch controls are not stated in the supplied quotes.
E1 covers staleness and reconciliation, but per-field ownership, a publication contract and a version are not stated in the supplied quotes.
E1 states the risk column is an original Tycho analysis, which entails that it is not a source-reported incident record.

items.notes: Thirty claim rows judged; core rows are directly supported by the gateway, limits and completion sections; partial rows name a missing semantic-owner, control-set or scope element.

claim_verdicts.reason: E1 says placing workers in different zones while keeping one unreplicated database does not satisfy a whole-journey failure objective; E2 denies that nominal placement diversity proves surviving journeys.

E2 states a container is not an availability zone, a managed service is not a business-state correctness proof and serverless autoscaling cannot create authoritative consistency; E1 says the deployment unit alone cannot answer the question.

E1 makes scale-to-demand conditional on the workload execution model; E2 lists runtime quotas/concurrency, start delay, state externalization, connection spikes, event retry/delivery and vendor control-plane/region dependencies.
E1 says capacity arriving after a short burst cannot prevent its initial overload; E2 says a new Pod can be running while its downstream database budget is exhausted.

E1 covers the finite-resource pool and the absence of added query capacity, and E2 covers platform threads, but 'or replicas' is not in this claim's quotes; the replica multiplication is carried by C6-E1.
E1 states increasing replicas can multiply backend connections beyond the database budget and turn local pool tuning into a shared failure.
E1 requires headroom for worst-case auto-scaling and failover; E2 requires accounting for peak replica count, not normal replica count.
E1 gives the ten-replica, 30-connection pool example requesting 300 connections and says a CPU-only scale-out can exhaust a fixed ceiling.

E1 is a general statement that correlated dependencies and measured time-to-recovery determine contract compliance; no supplied quote states that the incident refusal is application-owned connection multiplication or that it excludes a regional fault.
E1 defines a durable workflow as a persistent state machine whose steps, timers, retries, versions and compensation survive process loss; E2 requires explicit persistent state and failure contracts.
E1 says a reconnecting client must know which identity remains authoritative; E2 says the large-payload lifecycle must be designed independently of the database row.
E1 names at-least-once as a delivery contract and lists failures and late acknowledgments as duplicate causes, so duplicate delivery is expected rather than per se a provider failure.
E2 binds one logical intent, caller/payload scope and retention window to an authoritative outcome record; E1 makes idempotence a property of the intended effect.
E1 says an in-memory set deduplicates only in one live process and fails across replicas, restarts and retained events.

E2 requires external idempotency or durable reconciliation because a local database cannot make a remote effect atomic; E1 gives the loss/duplicate windows from marking before or after the external call.
E1 distinguishes event, business-command and effect identities, but no supplied quote establishes that the double charge is an effect-identity defect rather than a regional failure.

E1 gives the canonical boundary inventory to record separately: state writer, ingress, runtime instance, scheduler/control service, deployment mechanism, network path, secrets/identity service, availability zone/host/region and operator responsibility.

E1 says naming stateless workers a cell does not isolate a shared database, queue, cache or configuration publisher; E2 requires tracing every dependency and E3 names shared network/identity as a common failure mode.
E1 makes a regional exercise meaningful only with an explicit fault boundary; E2 limits a passing result to traffic and dependencies actually redirected; E3 states the disruption questions.
E1 supports multiple contributing causes in an after-action record, but 'attribution needs evidence rather than a convenient label' is not stated in the quote.
E1 requires the same observable outcome, admitted/offered load, logical data correctness and named outage, plus staffing, steady-state cost and a restore test.

E1 pins artifact/container, dependencies, data snapshot, tool version and test script; E2 requires equal offered-demand traces or disclosure and E3 equal arrival, skew, warm-up, pool, retries and cancellation.
E1 requires a comparable resource budget as well as a comparable offered workload; E2 says lower latency from twice the instances may be a capacity purchase.
E1 says different failure classes require distinct tests; E2 requires a safe abort condition.
E1 measures client-level correct outcomes, explicit rejections, timeouts, reconciliation, routed traffic, dependency recovery and total cost; E2 rejects green instance status as the metric.
E1 accepts the cheaper option only if it satisfies the same failure, cold-start and user-journey gates.
E1 returns insufficient evidence when the dominant failure class, transaction owner, placement domain, control-plane availability, workload shape or measured RPO/RTO is unknown.

E1 says a container or orchestration label does not establish fault isolation, useful spare capacity or recoverable state; E2 compares topologies on the same outcome, failure model, resource needs and operating capability.
E1 says all stateless frontends can become ineffective during a state-owner failure; E2 requires warmed capacity, routing, persisted state and duplicate-safe replay.
E1 frames the owning question as which workload, isolation and operating constraints make a runtime topology viable, not the compute-model label.

items.notes: Thirty claim rows judged; core rows on failure domains, state externalization, connection multiplication and effect identity are directly supported; the incident-attribution rows are partial because their quotes are general.

claim_verdicts.reason: E1 describes B's unconditional full-object replacement erasing A's title change; E2 says a last-writer timestamp can discard independent edits.
E1 states If-Match uses strong comparison, a failed condition normally produces 412, and its evaluation must not be an application-side read followed by an unguarded write.

E1 says two simultaneous first attempts cannot both pass a naive read-then-insert check; E2 says concurrent transactions can see the same capacity and E3 requires the check to be atomic with the mutation at the owner.
E1 states an ETag is a representation validator, not automatically a database row revision or content checksum; E2 requires a precondition tied to the state actually read.
E1 says conditional writes protect the scoped object operation and do not commit a separate database row; E2 states the scope of authoritative operations.
E3 says the data store, not application logic, must arbitrate a concurrent claim; E1 lists transaction/compare-and-set and E2 a durable uniqueness constraint or conditional write.
E1 says not to blindly retry a stale replacement with the latest validator; E2 explains a last-writer timestamp can discard independent edits.
E1 requires operation identity or a safe state-resolution protocol after a lost response and says a precondition failure on retry alone does not prove which attempt succeeded.
E1 says a precondition failure on retry alone does not prove which attempt succeeded; E2 distinguishes a receipt of stored edits from the observed frontier.
E1 says on a mismatch to reread and decide whether to merge or abandon; E2 gives the return-representation, submit-with-validator, atomically compare-and-mutate protocol.
E2 separates mergeable text from authoritative transitions; E1 says a union still violates the capacity invariant and E4 requires a transaction to enforce it.

E1 covers lost-response identity and E2 the receipt/frontier distinction, but no supplied quote states that the newest validator describes the already-damaged state or that a fresh validator cannot reveal or restore the lost edit.
E1 says a versioned schema is necessary but not sufficient; E2 lists the required acceptance cases and E3 requires untested guarantees to be stated as unresolved.

items.notes: Thirteen claim rows judged; core rows on preconditions, atomic compare-and-mutate, mismatch handling and lost responses are directly supported.

claim_verdicts.reason: E2 states pool parallelism removes per-key order unless partition assignment is explicit; E1 says several consumers read one queue and each message goes to one of them, processing in parallel.
E1 requires a stable key so an aggregate's events land in one partition and keep that partition's append sequence; E2 says partitioned consumers own a stable key range and preserve per-key order.
E2 rejects competing consumers when global order is mandatory or consumers mutate shared state without coordination; E1 also rejects strict global ordering without a partition key.
E1 says a group with more instances than assignable partitions cannot increase per-partition concurrent ownership.
E1 says a single hot key can concentrate traffic and limit parallel processing, and increasing partition count may not split that key.
E1 says a per-key worker pool preserves order only when partition assignment is stable; E2 requires a transition contract when key encoding or partition count changes.
E1 says stopping polling or a rebalance callback does not retract the remote request; E2 requires draining or classifying in-flight work and committing only resolved effects.
E1 states acknowledgment must follow the durable business effect and redelivery must not duplicate it; E2 says acknowledging before the effect can lose work.
E1 says committing before the external effect can lose it after a crash and committing after can duplicate it; E2 says no ordering of two independent commits creates a global transaction.

E2 says a crash after the effect but before acknowledgement can cause redelivery, requiring consumer-side deduplication and stable effect identity; E3 says redelivery resolves the previously recorded outcome.
E2 writes the deduplication marker and business side effects in the same transaction; E1 requires stable identity and atomic recording, and E3 requires a uniqueness constraint.
E2 requires the marker lifetime to cover maximum broker redelivery, DLQ replay and historical replay, and says a shorter window can duplicate the effect.

E1 says the handler must own effect identity, deduplication and acknowledgement ordering; E2 puts ordering in the subscription contract, not the framework default, and E3 commits only resolved positions.
E2 requires bounded attempts and a declared terminal path; E1 says an invalid schema or permanently rejected target is not repaired by retrying forever.

E1 classifies transient, permanent and unknown outcomes and preserves quarantine evidence; E2 says a dead-letter queue is a holding mechanism, not successful delivery or a safe replayer; E3 requires an owner, replay policy, bounded retention and alerting.
E3 requires an owner and replay policy, bounded retention and access, observable failure and alerting; E1 adds monitoring for silent abandonment and E2 retention longer than the source queue.
E1 says a poison record may stop the partition or skip data and requires a DLQ/quarantine contract, but 'reconcile before resuming' is not stated in the quote.
E2 says each current subscriber gets its own cursor; E1 supports independent reactions and E3 says fan-out cost grows with subscriber count.
E1 gives one ordered consumer per partition or a partitioned work queue and reverses the choice when ordering dominates throughput; E2 fits fan-out to independent subscribers needing a copy.
E1 allows buffering only with a reliable sequence domain, a bounded buffer, a gap timeout and a late-message disposition, and says to partition by key when global order is unnecessary.
E2 says a worker pool needs a visible in-flight count and a redelivery limit, not only higher prefetch; E1 says concurrency increases duplicate and reorder exposure.
E1 says a Kafka transaction does not automatically enclose an unrelated SQL commit, payment provider or email delivery; E2 says an offset is a replay position, not proof every effect succeeded.

E1 says a consumer acknowledgement retires the message after the redelivery policy; E2 says a publisher confirm means the broker accepted responsibility, not that the consumer completed the business effect.
E1 says message ordering is scoped to queue/subscription/stream/partition and concrete producer/consumer behavior, and no column implies global total order.

E1 says a crash after the local effect but before acknowledgement can cause redelivery and consumer-side deduplication is necessary for nonrepeatable effects; E2 says durable storage does not make the effect idempotent.
E1 requires the subscription to declare a prefetch or in-flight bound and an acknowledgement window, and to pause delivery or add capacity at the bound.
E1 says a queue dispatches each message to one eligible consumer and competing consumers share the work; E2 says a topic fans each publication out to every current matching subscriber.
E1 requires the queue contract to state its ordering scope and terminal path for poison messages; E2 requires a visible in-flight count and redelivery limit, not only prefetch.

E1 repeats with the same scoped idempotency identity and reconciles to the durable outcome; E2 surfaces an unknown outcome with bounded reconciliation or redesign, and E3 says blind retries cannot be guaranteed safe.
E1 describes the per-key transfer lock recognizing already-processed work; E3 says these defenses address duplicate work, not a magic end-to-end atomic transfer.

items.notes: Thirty claim rows judged; core rows on partitioning, acknowledgement order, duplicate identity and the terminal path are directly supported.

claim_verdicts.reason: E1 states in the current schema evidence.simulation carries the decision status by convention and describes the decision, not whether the simulation executed.

E1 says V12 keeps five layers separate, each answers a different question, results can be strong or weak per layer, the labels are not a ladder and a later layer never upgrades an earlier one; E2 says a model-verified label does not imply calibration.

E5 answers the model-verification question with units, conservation, boundary cases, event ordering and deterministic tests; E3 says a verified engine is not a validated system and E4 says tests do not prove operational validity.
E3 says every V12 model is uncalibrated, the inputs are assumed and the valid claim is conditional on the declared inputs; E1 gives the calibration question.

E2 says a decision-supported outcome with an uncalibrated model is conditional, follows from the declared assumptions and constraints, and does not say the assumptions are true; E4 gives the decision-layer question and reversal triggers.

E1 lists the record status as proposed, decision-supported, insufficient-evidence or rejected; E2 limits the decision status to decision-supported or insufficient-evidence, so the reviewer's imported decision-grade label is not a record value.

E1 says the simulation slot carries the decision status by convention; E2 gives the record status vocabulary, so agreement between the slot and the status it is specified to hold is identity, not independent corroboration.
E1 says V12 has no operational validation against a real system and every model records that limit; E4 says the models do not establish a match to a real system and E5 lists evidence inflation.

E1 says the operability constraint remains unverified and the recommendation is conditional; E2 forbids the safe-to-deploy inference, E3 denies owner acceptance, E4 denies pattern promotion and E5 states the limit.

E2 gives the model limits such as no dependency calls or storage, E3 the quadratic sensitivity screen, E4 the gate-order rule and E1 the untested operability constraint, but 'no operational validation' is not stated in this claim's quotes; it is carried by C8-E1.

E2 says more replications make the synthetic estimate more precise, not more representative; E1 says narrow intervals do not make inputs measured and E4 assigns convergence and replication to scenario and run records.

items.notes: Eleven claim rows judged; core rows on the slot map, the five separate layers and the narrow scope of decision-supported are directly supported.
